item.title: Experts urge stronger support for breastfeeding mothers
item.description: Amos Mpofu and Sikhulekelani Moyo, Zimpapers Reporters ZIMBABWE has joined more than 170 countries in commemorating World Breastfeeding Week, which began on Saturday and runs until August 7, with health experts calling for stronger family, workplace and community support systems to enable mothers to breastfeed successfully and improve child survival and development. This year’s global theme, Breastfeeding for a Sustainable Start in Life: Strengthen What Works, highlights the need to protect, promote and support breastfeeding as one of the most effective interventions for improving maternal and child health. Observed annually from August 1 to 7, World Breastfeeding Week is led by the World Alliance for Breastfeeding Action (WABA) in collaboration with the World Health Organisation (WHO), UNICEF and other partners. The campaign seeks to raise awareness of the lifelong health benefits of breastfeeding while encouraging governments, employers, healthcare providers and communities to create environments that enable mothers to breastfeed. President of the Paediatric Association of Zimbabwe, Dr Nyashadzashe Chasauka, said breastfeeding is one of the most powerful public health interventions available to reduce child mortality and promote healthy growth and development. Breastfeeding is the most important foundation in a child’s life, which is why Breastfeeding Week is an important week in our health calendar as it raises awareness on the importance of breastfeeding and advocates for support for breastfeeding mothers, he said. Breastfeeding is a strong start for a healthy and sustainable future for the baby and a mother’s milk is the first best gift of life. Breast milk is nutritious and protects babies from diarrhoeal diseases, chest infections and ear infections. Dr Chasauka said breastfeeding not only improves a child’s chances of survival during infancy but also contributes to healthier growth, stronger immunity and better development throughout life. According to the World Health Organisation, babies should be exclusively breastfed for the first six months, after which nutritious complementary foods should be introduced while breastfeeding continues until at least two years of age or beyond. Exclusive breastfeeding means infants receive only breast milk, without water, other liquids or foods, except prescribed medicines or vitamin supplements where necessary. Dr Chasauka also encouraged mothers living with HIV to breastfeed, saying modern treatment has significantly reduced the risk of mother-to-child transmission. All mothers can breastfeed, including mothers who are living with HIV. Mothers living with HIV need to adhere to their ARV treatment and babies given prophylactic medication during breastfeeding to prevent mother-to-child transmission, he said. Paediatrician and child health specialist Dr Wedu Ndebele said breastfeeding offers long-term health benefits that extend well beyond infancy. He said breastfed children are less likely to suffer from allergies, asthma and certain skin conditions while studies have also linked breastfeeding to improved brain development and cognitive performance. I hope everyone will talk about breastfeeding this week and encourage whether it’s your sister, your mother or your wife to breastfeed for the first six months without giving anything. We also encourage them to breastfeed up to two years of age if there’s no contraindication because those babies will grow very well, said Dr Ndebele. Registered nutritionist Ms Katinka Musavaya urged mothers experiencing breastfeeding difficulties to seek professional support instead of abandoning breastfeeding prematurely. Nourishing your baby from your breast is a powerful way to give them a strong start in life. No medicine, food or supplement is so perfectly crafted to suit your individual baby in your unique environment, and it’s free too, she said. Breastfeeding is natural, but it can also be exhausting and challenging. With the right support, you can overcome the hard days and feel confident in your breastfeeding journey. Ms Musavaya also expressed concern over increasing marketing of infant formula products, warning that aggressive advertising often undermines exclusive breastfeeding. She called for stricter enforcement of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, which seeks to regulate the promotion of infant formula and protect breastfeeding. We urge strict enforcement of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, and caution families that formula marketing is designed to sell a product, not to reflect medical necessity, she said. Nutritionist Mrs Annie Msauki Busumani said frequent breastfeeding, both day and night, is essential for establishing and maintaining an adequate milk supply. Breastfeeding day and night, on demand and without restricting frequency, is one of the most effective ways to build and sustain a mother’s milk supply. In our work with mothers across Zimbabwe, we have seen this simple, evidence-based practice work again and again, especially in those critical early weeks when supply is being established, she said. She said adolescent and teenage mothers often face unique challenges, including fear of disclosing their pregnancies, pressure from families and the need to return to school, factors that sometimes lead to mixed feeding instead of seeking professional guidance. Dietitian Ms Portia Chisvo said breastfeeding remains the gold standard for infant nutrition while also benefiting mothers. Breastfeeding gives babies the best nutrition and protection, and helps mothers recover too. Feed exclusively for the first six months, on demand with a good latch. Then continue with complementary foods up to two years and beyond. It’s nutrition, immunity and bonding all in one, she said. Zimbabwe has made significant progress in promoting exclusive breastfeeding through the Ministry of Health and Child Care, Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative and community-based nutrition programmes. Health authorities continue to encourage early initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour after birth and exclusive breastfeeding for six months as part of efforts to reduce child mortality, malnutrition and stunting. (via The Sunday News) #Zimbabwe #ZimbabweNews

item.title: Sewing hope: Insiza North women get 30 machines to fight poverty @ZANUPF_Official
item.description: Dorothy N Sithole Thirty women’s groups in Insiza North have received a major boost after being equipped with sewing machines to manufacture reusable sanitary pads and other garments as part of efforts to promote self-reliance and fight poverty in rural communities. The machines were handed over at Ensangu Primary School Village 5 on Saturday, with beneficiaries from Nyozane, Lochard and Shangani wards receiving 10 machines each, together with fabric, thread and scissors. The initiative, supported by American philanthropist Mrs Julie Phippen through the Methodist Church, is aimed at helping women generate income while improving access to affordable sanitary wear for schoolgirls and elderly women. The handover ceremony was attended by a Bulawayo Diocese delegation led by Rev Sinini Ndiweni, Elder Mthokozisi Stephen Dube and Church Coordinator Mrs Isabel Ndebele, as well as local leaders including Ward 22 Councillor Cde Kinani Dlodlo and Methodist Church Ensangu Block 5 minister Rev Alister Mashoko. Speaking during the event, Mrs Ndebele said the donation was about restoring dignity and creating sustainable opportunities rather than providing temporary assistance. This promise is here today, but these do not belong to individuals. They belong to you, the community, she said. Church leaders said the project was designed to address poverty, reduce challenges faced by girls who miss school due to lack of sanitary wear, and empower women through income-generating activities. Elder Dube described the sewing machines as a gateway to economic independence. This machine is not just metal. It is a door. Walk through it together, he said. To promote inclusivity and prevent disputes, leaders agreed that the machines would be housed at nearby schools instead of individual homes, allowing women from different backgrounds to access them. Mrs Ndebele said placing the machines in one household could create divisions within communities. “If we keep them in one homestead, jealousy kills projects,” she said. She said every woman, regardless of religious affiliation, should benefit from the initiative. Apart from producing reusable sanitary pads, beneficiaries will also be trained to make school uniforms and other garments, expanding opportunities for income generation. Mrs Phippen pledged the donation after visiting Zimbabwe and hearing women speak about the challenges associated with the high cost and limited availability of sanitary products. The event also received additional support, with ward 23 shadow councillor, Cde Sikhanyisiwe Nkomo donating US$100 to an orphaned schoolgirl and US$60 to the Shangani group towards transport costs. Rev Ndiweni, who delivered a sermon from Psalms 127, urged beneficiaries and community leaders to work together for the success of the project. Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labour in vain. Let us build together, with one spirit, he said. Matabeleland South Zanu PF Women’s League provincial secretary Cde Clara Langa described the initiative as a practical contribution towards the attainment of Vision 2030. The day ended with songs and celebrations as beneficiaries received their sewing machines, marking what leaders described as a new chapter of empowerment for women in Insiza North. (via The Sunday News) #Zimbabwe #ZimbabweNews
